title: In Brief: New Documentary Seeks Atlantis in Scandinavia

content:
As I continue to work on my book proposal, I only have time for a brief notice today: A new English-language documentary about to have is German premiere is going in search of Atlantis in one of the least likely spots: Scandinavia. If that sounds a little familiar, it's because it's based on early modern Swedish scholar Olof Rudbeck's eccentric theory, which had its heyday in the seventeenth century. Fortunately, it seems that the team behind the hour-long film, which is produced and directed by Bernhard Shirg, who teaches public history and has a PhD in Renaissance Latin, are more interested in the social history of how Europeans understood the far north than in finding Atlantis itself. The press release for the film describes it this way:

In the 1670s, the Swedish polymath Olof Rudbeck the Elder attempted to prove that the utopian places described in classical mythology were located in Scandinavia. Dr. Bernhard Schirg of the University of Hamburg followed in Rudbeck’s footsteps and traces his imaginary geography in his film “Frozen Atlantis – Seeking Wonder in Shifting Lands.”“Frozen Atlantis” is a cinematic essay produced as part of a “Freigeist” grant from the Volkswagen Foundation. In it, Renaissance scholar Bernhard Schirg sets out in search of the wondrous that people have found in their world throughout the ages—a poetic journey through the inner and outer landscapes of the 21st century that explores the human need for belonging, connection, and stories.

On his journey through Sweden’s mountains, rivers, and glaciers, Bernhard Schirg—guided by 17th-century books, maps, and panoramic sketches—follows in the footsteps of Olof Rudbeck the Elder (1630–1702). Over the course of three decades, Rudbeck had expanded his thesis and, in his monumental work *Atlantica*, asserted that all ancient myths originated in the North and that the cradle of civilization lay there.

Together with explorer Lars Larsson, Bernhard Schirg ventures into landscapes that Rudbeck claimed formed the basis for myths such as Atlantis and Elysium. His journey thus becomes a search for answers to the question of what perspectives these myths once anchored in the nature of the North.
​
Rudbeck’s holistic vision and narrative of the Swedish landscapes are contrasted with the transformative influence of humankind. Through its interventions in nature, humankind continually alters what Rudbeck once described as immutable. “Frozen Atlantis” raises the question of how the stories we tell shape our relationship to the world around us. Can myths—even in the post-truth era—inspire new perspectives—perspectives that move us?

According to the University of Hamburg, where Shirg teaches, he has been studying Rudbeck and his vision of Atlantis since 2021 and the documentary is a public-facing part of the Volkswagen Foundation-funded research.
